Vance Mocks Epstein Files Heckler as Illegal Immigrant at N.C. Rally

by Veronika Kyrylenko October 19, 2026
Share
Login to Listen
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:56
Instaread

Another protester called for the release of Jeffrey Epstein’s files at a Republican rally on Monday. This time, it was in North Carolina, where Vice President JD Vance was headlining a midterm campaign event. Rather than address the issue, Vance turned the interruption into a joke, suggesting the man was an illegal immigrant.

The confrontation came exactly one week after another protester displaying the same message was physically attacked by several men at a rally headlined by President Donald Trump in Ohio.

Both incidents involved a demand that Trump and Vance themselves had championed before taking office.

The Heckling

The confrontation occurred at the Hyder Warehouse in Hendersonville, North Carolina. Vance appeared to support Republican congressional candidate Jennifer Balkcom in North Carolina’s competitive 11th Congressional District. The event was part of a broader Republican campaign effort to mobilize voters before Election Day.

The video footage shows the vice president speaking at a podium with supporters seated behind him.

Vance was criticizing what he called a “corrupt, far-left cartel” when a man directly behind him suddenly stood and interrupted.

“God bless our children!” the protester shouted. “Release the Epstein files!”

Vance turned toward the protester as the audience booed, then broke into chants of “USA! USA!” Security personnel moved in to escort the man out.

Instead of addressing the substance of the protest, Vance responded with a reference to his administration’s immigration record:

Ladies and gentlemen, I’m gonna have to amend something I said earlier. I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America.

He smiled and added, “But one isn’t bad, right?”

The remark suggested that the brown-skinned protester had entered the country illegally, a peculiar insinuation unless Vance happened to know the man and his immigration history personally. More striking was the implication of his joke: that demanding transparency about the sexual trafficking of children was something an illegal immigrant, rather than an American citizen, would do. The crowd’s chants of “USA” reinforced the suggestion that the protester’s demand was somehow un-American.

The audience’s patriotic chanting continued as security escorted the man away.

Vance’s Record

Long before he became vice president, JD Vance publicly questioned why the government was withholding information about Jeffrey Epstein and his powerful associates.

In September 2021, Vance wrote on Twitter:

Remember when we learned that our wealthiest and most powerful people were connected to a guy who ran a literal child sex trafficking ring? And then that guy died mysteriously in jail. And now we just don’t talk about it.

A few months later, responding to a claim that the Justice Department (DOJ) and Ghislaine Maxwell’s lawyers had agreed to keep Epstein’s address book secret, Vance posed another pointed question:

What possible interest would the US government have in keeping Epstein’s clients secret? Oh…

He returned to the subject during the 2024 presidential campaign. Appearing on comedian Theo Von’s This Past Weekend podcast on October 22, he remarked that politicians often had vices worse than alcoholism.

“Release the list!” Von interjected.

Vance laughed, then responded:

Seriously, we need to release the Epstein list. That is an important thing. We can go down that rabbit hole.

Once in office, Vance continued to profess support for transparency. During a June 2026 appearance on ABC’s The View, he described himself as “kind of a conspiracy theorist on the Epstein stuff” and insisted, “I wanted to have full transparency.”

In July, he acknowledged on Joe Rogan’s podcast that the administration had mishandled the release:

If people want to say we mishandled the Epstein release, guilty.

Thus, the demand shouted in Hendersonville was hardly unfamiliar to Vance. It was one he had repeatedly made himself.

A Week Earlier

The Hendersonville incident followed a violent confrontation at an October 12 campaign rally headlined by Trump in Youngstown, Ohio.

A woman wearing a “Release the Epstein Files” shirt interrupted Trump’s speech and was attacked by male attendees. A widely circulated video showed one man shoving her, punching her face, and pulling her hair. Nearby supporters chanted “USA.” Police removed the woman, while her attacker remained and exchanged high-fives with other attendees.

Trump accused her without evidence of being a paid protester and mocked her appearance.

No evidence has emerged that the woman initiated the violence, although footage does not establish everything that preceded the assault.

Youngstown Police Lt. Frank Rutherford told HuffPost, “If you punch somebody in the face, you should get in trouble for that.”

Authorities made no arrests. The sheriff said deputies had not witnessed the assault and the woman declined to file a complaint.

Heckling may justify removing a protester. It does not justify assault. Yet the recorded response included cheers for the attacker and ridicule from the president.

The Epstein Files: Promises and Resistance

The Epstein affair extends far beyond any “ordinary” political scandal. At its center are the sexual trafficking and abuse of minors and Epstein’s connections to powerful figures in politics, business, academia, and finance. The disclosures have also raised questions about intelligence connections, reproductive exploitation, genetic engineering, pandemic networks, cannibalism, and occult and satanic rituals.

After months of resisting disclosure and dismissing the controversy as a “Democrat hoax,” Trump reversed course under overwhelming bipartisan pressure. In November 2025, he signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, requiring the DOJ to release its records within 30 days and prohibiting politically motivated withholding.

The department missed that deadline. In January 2026, it announced the release of approximately 3.5 million pages, but delays, redactions, and initially withheld FBI interviews fueled further scrutiny.

The resistance continued in court. In Phang v. Blanche, a federal judge ordered DOJ to release additional records or justify withholding them. The department challenged aspects of that order and sought relief while appealing.

Meanwhile, at Trump’s and Vance’s rallies, Americans demanding the very transparency their leaders once promised are met with ridicule, removal, and, in Ohio, physical violence.
